While Australian rules football in Ireland has a limited following, a series of International rules football games (constituting a hybrid of the Australian and Gaelic football codes) takes place annually between teams representing Ireland and Australia. Baseball and basketball are also emerging sports in Ireland, both of which have an international team representing the island of Ireland. Other sports which retain a following in Ireland include cycling, greyhound racing, horse riding, and motorsport.
In 2011, Ireland was ranked the most charitable country in Europe, and second most charitable in the world.

A constitutional ban on divorce was lifted following a referendum in 1995. Divorce rates in Ireland are very low compared to European Union averages (0.7 divorced people per 1,000 population in 2011) while the marriage rate in Ireland is slightly above the European Union average (4.6 marriages per 1,000 population per year in 2012). Abortion had been banned throughout the period of the Irish state, first through provisions of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and later by the Protection of Life During Pregnancy Act 2013. The right to life of the unborn was protected in the constitution by the Eighth Amendment in 1983; this provision was removed following a referendum, and replaced it with a provision allowing legislation to regulate the termination of pregnancy. The Health (Regulation of Termination of Pregnancy) Act 2018 passed later that year provided for abortion generally during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, and in specified circumstances after that date. Capital punishment is constitutionally banned in Ireland, while discrimination based on age, gender, sexual orientation, marital or familial status, religion, race or membership of the travelling community is illegal. The legislation which outlawed homosexual acts was repealed in 1993. The Civil Partnership and Certain Rights and Obligations of Cohabitants Act 2010 permitted civil partnerships between same-sex couples. The Children and Family Relationships Act 2015 allowed for adoption rights for couples other than married couples, including civil partners and cohabitants, and provided for donor-assisted human reproduction; however, significant sections of the Act have yet to be commenced. Following a referendum held on 23 May 2015, Ireland became the eighteenth country to provide in law for same-sex marriage, and the first to do so by popular vote. Ireland became the first country in the world to introduce an environmental levy for plastic shopping bags in 2002 and a public smoking ban in 2004. Recycling in Ireland is carried out extensively, and Ireland has the second highest rate of packaging recycling in the European Union. It was the first country in Europe to ban incandescent lightbulbs in 2008 and the first EU country to ban in-store tobacco advertising and product display in 2009. In 2015, Ireland became the second country in the world to introduce plain cigarette packaging. Despite the above measures to discourage tobacco use, smoking rates in Ireland remain at approximately 15.4% as of 2020.

Although originally published in English in 1912, the song was translated into Irish in 1923 and the Irish-language version is more commonly sung today.

The first four bars of the chorus followed by the last five comprise the presidential salute. The arms of Ireland originate as the arms of the monarchs of Ireland and was recorded as the arms of the King of Ireland in the 12th century. From the union of the crowns of England, Scotland and Ireland in 1603, they have appeared quartered on the royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom. Today, they are the personal arms of the president of Ireland whilst he or she is in office and are flown as the presidential standard.
Its complex and layered past stretches from prehistoric settlements to its current role as a modern European democracy.
Human presence in Ireland dates back to around 10,000 BCE during the Mesolithic era, with evidence of early hunter-gatherer communities found in sites such as Mount Sandel in County Londonderry.
These tombs, older than the Egyptian pyramids, indicate a highly organized and spiritual society.

Celtic culture, arriving around 500 BCE, laid the foundation for the Gaelic language and social structures that dominated Ireland for centuries. Ireland was not unified under one government but divided into tuatha, or tribal kingdoms, each ruled by a chieftain. These Gaelic societies developed rich oral traditions, preserved by bards and druids, and organized their society through the Brehon Laws, a sophisticated and customary legal system based on restitution and community standing. During this time, Irish mythology flourished with tales such as the Táin Bó Cúailnge and the exploits of mythic heroes like Cú Chulainn and Fionn mac Cumhaill, stories that continue to be central to Irish cultural identity.
The arrival of Christianity in the 5th century CE marked a turning point in Irish history.

Beginning in the 8th century, Viking raids targeted monastic sites and coastal settlements, culminating in the establishment of Norse towns such as Dublin, Waterford, Wexford, Cork, and Limerick. Over time, many Vikings assimilated into Irish society. The 12th century brought a more significant and long-lasting foreign presence: the Anglo-Normans. At the behest of the deposed Irish king Diarmait Mac Murchada, Norman forces led by Richard de Clare, known as Strongbow, landed in 1169.
By the late Middle Ages, the English Crown had established the Pale, a region of direct control centered around Dublin, while Gaelic lords retained power in much of the island.
The Nine Years' War (1594–1603) and the Flight of the Earls in 1607 marked the end of Gaelic aristocratic resistance and the collapse of the old Gaelic order.

The 17th century was a period of immense suffering for the Irish population. The Cromwellian conquest (1649–1653) led to mass killings, land confiscation, and famine. The subsequent Williamite Wars in the 1690s entrenched Protestant Ascendancy rule, marginalizing the Catholic majority through the Penal Laws. These laws restricted Catholic rights to education, property ownership, political participation, and religious practice.

The 18th century, though still marked by inequality, saw the emergence of a growing sense of Irish national identity among both Catholics and Protestants. The Protestant-led Patriot movement sought greater autonomy from Britain, culminating in the establishment of an independent Irish Parliament in 1782, though this independence was limited and short-lived. The 1790s saw the rise of revolutionary republicanism, inspired by the American and French revolutions.
The 1798 Rebellion, however, was brutally suppressed, and the failure of this uprising led to the 1801 Act of Union, which merged Ireland with Great Britain to form the United Kingdom.

This catastrophic event left deep scars on Irish society and significantly shaped Irish nationalism. The rise of cultural nationalism in the late 19th century saw the Gaelic Revival promote the Irish language, traditional sports, and folklore. Organizations such as the Gaelic Athletic Association and the Gaelic League became cornerstones of national identity. Parallel to this was the push for political self-determination, first through constitutional means via Home Rule movements and later through revolutionary action.
The early 20th century marked a dramatic shift in the struggle for Irish independence.
In the 1918 general election, Sinn Féin, advocating for full independence, won a landslide victory.
This led to the Irish War of Independence (1919–1921), a guerrilla conflict between the Irish Republican Army and British forces.
The Free State prevailed, but the conflict left a legacy of bitterness and political fragmentation. Over the next two decades, Ireland gradually severed its ties with the British Commonwealth.

The mid-to-late 20th century was a period of economic and social transformation. For much of this time, Ireland remained relatively poor and economically dependent on agriculture. Emigration continued to be a defining feature of Irish life. However, beginning in the 1960s, modernization efforts brought industrial development, educational reform, and greater urbanization. Ireland remained officially neutral during World War II, a policy known as “The Emergency,” which was characterized by strict censorship and resource rationing.

The Northern Ireland conflict, known as The Troubles, had profound effects on the Republic. Though the violence was largely confined to Northern Ireland, the Republic played a role in peace efforts and provided refuge to many. The Good Friday Agreement in 1998, which brought an end to most of the violence, was supported by the Republic of Ireland and remains a landmark achievement in Anglo-Irish relations.

This boom significantly improved living standards and allowed for the development of infrastructure, technology sectors, and urban renewal. However, the global financial crisis of 2008 hit Ireland hard, leading to a banking collapse, IMF-EU bailout, and years of austerity. Despite this, Ireland recovered in the 2010s and continues to be one of the fastest-growing economies in the Eurozone.

Modern Ireland is a pluralistic and democratic society with a vibrant culture and dynamic global presence. Irish identity has been reshaped by immigration, EU membership, social liberalization, and ongoing engagement with the diaspora. Major social changes in the 21st century include the legalization of same-sex marriage in 2015 and the repeal of the constitutional ban on abortion in 2018, both following national referendums. The Irish language, while not widely spoken as a first language, remains a key symbol of cultural heritage and is taught in schools and used in official contexts.

Culturally, Ireland remains world-renowned for its contributions to literature, music, theater, and the arts. Writers such as James Joyce, W.B. Yeats, Samuel Beckett, and Seamus Heaney have earned global acclaim, and contemporary Irish authors continue to win prestigious literary awards.
Irish cinema and television have gained international recognition, with actors, directors, and writers making significant contributions to global media.
Its political landscape has evolved from historical divisions rooted in the Civil War to a more diversified spectrum, including progressive and centrist parties.

The reintroduction of border controls remains a sensitive issue due to the peace agreement and the economic interdependence of the island. Ireland’s position in the European Union, its strong commitment to human rights, and its strategic role in transatlantic relations position it as a key player in both European and global affairs.

In essence, the Republic of Ireland is a nation built on a legacy of endurance, creativity, and profound cultural depth. Its journey from colonization and famine to independence and economic success reflects a remarkable narrative of national rebirth. The modern Republic of Ireland continues to draw strength from its history while embracing change, remaining a nation deeply connected to its past but actively shaping its future.
